title: Black theology
hookLine: James Cone saw the cross in the lynching tree and God on the side of the oppressed

lines: A QUESTION THAT WOULD NOT LEAVE.
cards: An old spiritual asks a question that seems to have no date on it: "Were you there when they crucified my Lord?"

Tradition traces songs like it, the spirituals this path met earlier, to Black Christians in America, singing under slavery. James Cone grew up in Black churches in the American South, where songs like that were sung.
As a theologian, he asked a question that would not leave him alone. If Jesus was a man executed on a tree, what does the cross say to people who watched their neighbors hanged from trees?

teach.b: Cone's fullest answer came in a book called The Cross and the Lynching Tree. His point was plain. Rome crucified Jesus in public, as a warning, the kind of death the empire used to humiliate people it wanted to crush.
Lynching in America, Cone wrote, was public too, a warning to Black communities, often with a crowd looking on. The two trees, he said, belong side by side, and he pressed the church to look at both.
The New Testament itself calls the cross a tree.

teach.h: IN HIS OWN BODY ON THE TREE.
teach.b: The first letter of Peter says that Christ "his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree." Cone read that word with American history in his ears. His second claim was about God.
In Exodus, God speaks from the burning bush: "I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows."
Cone kept returning to lines like that. God sees. God hears.
God takes the side of those who are crushed. That's what he meant by Black theology: the gospel heard from inside a people's suffering and their struggle to be free.
And he held to Easter: the one hanged on the tree was raised. Christians read Cone in different ways.
He kept coming back to the old spiritual, and to its question, which is put to every listener: were you there?

how: In some Black churches, preaching and song hold Christ's suffering together with the community's own history, and spirituals such as "Were You There" are sung in Holy Week; Cone's books are read in seminaries and churches.

games.q: you're a preacher. people in your pews have seen neighbors lynched. this week you're preaching on the cross. what do you do?
o: preach the cross as something that happened far away.
set the cross beside the lynching tree.
skip the cross and preach on something gentler.
games.why: that was the road Cone's theology took: the two trees side by side, and God on the side of those who are crushed. he held to Easter too: the one hanged on the tree was raised.

practice: Bring to mind one place where people are being crushed, a neighborhood, a country, a prison, or one person you know, and let it be real for a moment without rushing past.
If you pray, you can hold them before the God who says, in Exodus, I have heard their cry, in your own words or in silence; if you don't, hold them in mind and ask what one small thing you could do.
